slides.title:
Sony's bosses asked:
who buys a player
that *can't record?*
slides.sub:
30,000 people. In two months.
Then over 200 million 👇

slides.title:
Sony co-founder Masaru Ibuka
wants to hear opera on
his flights. His recorder
is *too heavy*.
slides.sub:
He asks for a small stereo player
for his next trip to the US
(History.com, Sound & Vision).

slides.title:
Engineers rip the speaker
and record button out of
a Pressman recorder.
*Stereo only.*
slides.sub:
Kozo Ohsone's team builds the first
prototype in four days
(Sound & Vision, Mental Floss).

slides.title:
No Sony tape deck had ever
sold more than that.
Inside, people were
*skeptical*.
slides.sub:
The big objection: who wants a
cassette player that can't record?
(Sound & Vision, History.com)

slides.title:
Chairman Akio Morita orders
30,000 units. If they don't
sell out, he says he'll
*resign*.
slides.sub:
Launch: July 1, 1979, in Japan.
About ¥30,000 (History.com,
Sound & Vision, Mental Floss).

slides.title:
sold in July. So Sony puts
it *in people's hands*,
right on the street.
slides.sub:
Staff let Tokyo pedestrians listen
and wear them on trains
(History.com, TechSpot).

slides.title: Don't you think a stereo cassette player that you can listen to *while walking around* is a good idea?
slides.author:
Masaru Ibuka, Sony co-founder,
answering the doubters (via History.com)

slides.title:
All 30,000 gone by the
end of August. Then
the world *walks with music*.
slides.sub:
Over 200 million cassette Walkmans
sold before production ended in 2010
(TechSpot; Mental Floss says 385M).

slides.title:
Don't explain it.
Let them *try it*.
slides.sub:
Specs didn't sell the Walkman.
One minute with headphones did.
